task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper explainer for general readers answering the question: How does antibiotic resistance develop, and why is the pipeline of new antibiotics so thin? Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of March 14, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria evolve mechanisms to survive exposure to a drug; the mechanisms include pumping the antibiotic out of the cell, chemically neutralizing it, or modifying the cellular target the drug attacks.
Resistance is a natural evolutionary process that occurs without human action, but overuse and misuse of antibiotics accelerates it by creating selection pressure that favors resistant bacteria.
A single bacterium can pass resistance genes not just to its own descendants but to entirely unrelated bacterial species through a process called horizontal gene transfer.
Drug-resistant infections kill an estimated 1.27 million people worldwide per year and contribute to 4.95 million deaths in which they are a contributing factor, according to a 2022 Lancet study.

Gram-negative bacteria — a class that includes E. coli, Klebsiella, and Pseudomonas — are particularly difficult to treat because their outer membrane acts as a second barrier that excludes many antibiotics.

The carbapenem class of antibiotics is considered a last resort for gram-negative infections; bacteria resistant to carbapenems (carbapenem-resistant organisms, or CROs) are considered a critical public health threat by the WHO.

Infectious disease researcher Dr. Victor Ogede of Northgate University said: "We have been relying on modifications of existing antibiotic classes for decades. Truly new mechanisms of action are extraordinarily rare and take 10 to 15 years to develop."

The economics of antibiotic development are unfavorable: new antibiotics are used sparingly (to preserve their effectiveness), taken for short courses, and often face competition from older generic drugs priced at cents per dose.

Several large pharmaceutical companies have exited antibiotic research because the expected return on investment does not justify the development cost; small companies often cannot sustain operations long enough to bring a drug to market.
The WHO maintains a priority pathogen list of bacteria for which new treatments are urgently needed; carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii is in the critical tier.
Pull incentives — market rewards paid when a drug is approved and used — are being piloted in the United Kingdom and proposed in U.S. legislation; they aim to decouple revenue from sales volume.

Agricultural use of antibiotics — particularly growth promoters in livestock — has been a significant driver of resistance globally; the EU has banned growth-promoting uses, and the U.S. has restricted them.
Dr. Ogede said resistance surveillance — tracking which drugs are failing in hospitals — is inadequate in low- and middle-income countries, where most deaths from resistant infections occur.

Bacteriophage therapy — using viruses that specifically kill bacteria — is an experimental alternative being used in compassionate use cases where antibiotics have failed; it is not an approved therapy in most countries.
Hospital infection control — hand hygiene, isolation of infected patients, and targeted prescribing — remains the most evidence-based tool for slowing the spread of resistant organisms.

Rapid diagnostic tests that can identify the bacterial species and its resistance profile within hours, rather than days, allow doctors to prescribe the right antibiotic sooner and avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum use.
Dr. Ogede said the lag between a drug entering clinical trials and reaching the market is 10 to 15 years, meaning the drugs needed for 2040 would need to begin development now.
The ESKAPE pathogens — Enterococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella, Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, and Enterobacter — are the six species responsible for most drug-resistant hospital infections.
Global coordination on antibiotic stewardship is limited; some countries require prescriptions for antibiotics while others sell them over the counter without restriction.
Dr. Ogede said climate change may worsen resistance by expanding the geographic range of resistant organisms and increasing the frequency of infectious disease outbreaks that drive antibiotic use.
